blocks.text: When a client connects to an MCP server, it has no idea yet what that server can offer as resources.
Resource discovery is the process of asking the server to describe its resources, so the client knows what exists before it ever reads anything.
This lesson walks through the resources/list request, what a client learns from the response, and how a server can tell a client when the picture has changed.
1. Why Resource Discovery Matters
An MCP server can expose anything from a single file to thousands of database rows as resources.
Without a discovery step, a client would have to guess resource URIs blindly, which simply does not scale.
Discovery turns that guessing game into a straightforward request and response, the same way a directory listing tells you what files exist before you open one.

blocks.title: Think of it like a menu
blocks.content: A restaurant menu tells you what dishes exist before you order one. resources/list is that menu for an MCP server.

blocks.text: 2. The resources/list Request
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440483681-55399841.png
Discovery begins with the client sending a resources/list request over the same JSON-RPC channel used for everything else in MCP.
The request itself is small, it barely needs any parameters at all.
Some servers support an optional cursor parameter for paging through a long list, which we will touch on further down.
3. The resources/list Response
The server answers with a result object containing a resources array.
Every entry in that array describes one resource the client is now allowed to read.
Nothing has been read yet at this point, the client only knows what is available.
4. Resource URIs: The Identifier the Client Keeps
Each resource entry carries a uri field, and that string is the one thing the client must hold onto.
The uri is what gets passed to a later resources/read call to actually fetch the content.
A client should treat the uri as an opaque token, not something to parse apart and reinterpret on its own.
5. Metadata: Name, Description, and mimeType
Alongside the uri, a resource entry carries a small bundle of metadata that helps a client, or a human using the client, decide what to do with it.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Purpose"],"rows":[["name","A short, human readable label for the resource"],["description","A sentence or two explaining what the resource contains"],["mimeType","The content type, so the client knows how to interpret the bytes once read"]]}

blocks.text: None of these fields are required to be unique, and none of them are used to fetch the resource, that job belongs entirely to the uri.
6. Discovery Happens Before Reading
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440483681-377992755.png
Discovery and reading are two separate steps, and MCP keeps them cleanly split apart on purpose.
resources/list only returns metadata, it never returns the actual content of a resource.
A client has to make a second, separate resources/read call, passing the exact uri it learned about, to get the real bytes.

blocks.title: Why split them
blocks.content: Listing a thousand resources is cheap. Reading the content of all one thousand up front would not be. Splitting the steps keeps discovery fast even when the underlying data is large.

blocks.text: 7. Listing at Startup vs Listing on Demand
Some clients call resources/list once, right after connecting, and cache the result for the rest of the session.
Other clients call it on demand, for example only when a user opens a resource picker in the interface.
Both approaches are valid, and MCP does not mandate either one, a server simply has to be ready to answer resources/list whenever it is asked.

items: Startup listing gives a client an instant picture of everything available, useful for building a sidebar or menu right away.
On demand listing avoids doing work the user may never need, useful when a server has a very large or expensive to compute resource set.
A client can also mix both, an initial quick call followed by refreshed calls later.

blocks.text: 8. Discovery Inside the Session Lifecycle
Resource discovery does not happen in isolation, it sits inside the broader connection lifecycle between a client and a server.
The client and server first complete an initialize handshake, during which the server declares whether it supports resources at all.
Only after that handshake does it make sense for a client to call resources/list, since calling it against a server with no resources capability would be pointless.
9. Declaring the Resources Capability
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440483681-430843473.png
During initialize, a server that supports resources includes a resources object in its capabilities.
The listChanged flag tells the client whether this server can send the resources/list_changed notification, which we cover next.
10. The resources/list_changed Notification
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440483682-29956345.png
A server's resource set is not always fixed forever, files get created, database rows get added, tickets get closed.
When the underlying set changes, a server that declared listChanged can send a notification telling the client its cached list is now stale.
Notice there is no id field, this is a notification, not a request, so the client does not reply to it.
11. How a Client Should React to list_changed
The notification itself carries no details about what changed, only that something did.
The correct client behavior is simple, call resources/list again and replace the cached list with the fresh result.
A client should never try to guess what changed from the notification alone, since the message intentionally carries no diff.
12. Discovery Is Repeatable, Not One Time

blocks.alt: Discovery Is Repeatable, Not One Time
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440584718-558930031.png
It helps to think of resources/list as a query you can run again at any point, not a one time handshake step.
A long running client might call it once at startup, then again after every list_changed notification, then again if the user explicitly asks to refresh.
Nothing about calling it a second time is unusual, the server simply answers with whatever is current at that moment.
13. Paging Through Large Resource Lists
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440584719-410443613.png
When a server has far too many resources to return in one response, it can use cursor based pagination.
The response includes a nextCursor field when there is more to fetch, and the client passes that value back on the following call.
A client should keep calling resources/list with the returned cursor until no nextCursor comes back, at which point the full set has been collected.
14. A Minimal Client Discovering Resources
Here is a small example of a client function that discovers every resource a server exposes, following the cursor until the list is complete.
This function only collects metadata, it never touches resources/read, discovery and reading stay cleanly separate.
15. Reacting to Changes in Python
The same pattern shows up in a Python client that listens for the list_changed notification and refreshes its cache.
Notice the handler does not try to figure out what changed, it simply refetches and replaces.
16. Discovery Versus Templates
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440584719-217412689.png
resources/list only returns concrete resources that already exist right now.
Some servers additionally expose resource templates, parameterized patterns a client can fill in to construct a uri itself.
Templates are a separate mechanism, discovery of concrete resources through resources/list is the simpler and more common case, and the one this lesson focuses on.
17. Worked Example
Imagine a note taking server that exposes three markdown files as resources.
The client connects, completes initialize, sees resources.listChanged is true, and calls resources/list.
A minute later, the user creates a new note called groceries.md through some other interface entirely.
The server notices the new file and sends notifications/resources/list_changed.
The client, following the rule from section eleven, calls resources/list again and now sees four resources instead of three.
Common Mistakes

items: Calling resources/read before ever calling resources/list, guessing at a uri instead of discovering it.
Ignoring the listChanged capability flag and never refreshing a cached list, so the client silently drifts out of date.
Trying to extract details of what changed from the list_changed notification itself, when the message intentionally carries none.
Stopping pagination early and assuming the first page is the full resource set.
Parsing the internal structure of a resource uri on the client side instead of treating it as an opaque string.

blocks.text: Practice

Write a short client function in the language of your choice that calls resources/list, prints each resource's name and mimeType, and then registers a handler that recalls resources/list whenever a list_changed notification arrives.
Test it against a mental model of a server that starts with two resources and gains a third partway through your session.
Key Takeaway
Resource discovery is just the resources/list request and response, a small array of uris plus metadata, sitting inside the larger client and server session.
Keep discovery and reading separate, refetch the list whenever a list_changed notification arrives, and treat every uri as an opaque handle to pass back later.
